S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, property damage, or emergency service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, with a detailed report within 10 calendar days. They must notify affected customers within 5 calendar days when an incident indicates a potential safety hazard for their model, and promptly provide material updates. Reports must include model, incident date, known consequences, and available cause information.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Manufacturers must submit per-model results and test-method details to the relevant regulator and provide the per-model results to customers who buy that model. Exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit marketing; the regulator may require additional measures, including suspension or withdrawal, if it determines the model presents an unreasonable safety risk.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before initial marketing and after any material design change. Manufacturers must submit per-model results and test-method details to the relevant regulator and provide the per-model results to customers who buy that model. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt regulator notification, a documented corrective-action plan, and retesting on a regulator-approved schedule. Exceeding 5% alone does not automatically prohibit marketing; the regulator may require additional measures, including suspension or withdrawal, if it determines the model presents an unreasonable safety risk. Customers must also receive relevant safety instructions and material hazard notices.

S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New home battery models must support remote emergency shut-off no later than 24 months after adoption. S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Customers must receive clear safety notices describing material hazards, safe operation, incident-reporting contacts, and corrective actions relevant to their model; manufacturers must provide material updates promptly. When any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers and provide the supporting model-level data. The exceedance triggers a regulator review and a documented manufacturer corrective-action plan. A recall is required when the regulator determines, based on the incident data and risk assessment, that a recall is necessary to address an unreasonable safety risk. Regulators receive model-level incident and recall data; public notices must identify affected products and actions, but need not publish per-model test failure rates.

judge_section_notes: The final S2 keeps the 5% failure rate as a corrective-action and retesting trigger rather than a sales ban, so sales never have to stop automatically, and it gives customers per-model numeric results. S3 delays new-unit shut-off to 24 months and sets a 6-year retrofit window with a safety-plan escape, and S5 makes recall discretionary with no numeric recall trigger, the 8/100k threshold only prompting notice, review and corrective action. S1 is the strongest section, with 24-hour reporting of all thermal incidents and 5-day customer notice.
